questions.stem: What makes transport through nuclear pore complexes directional?

options.B: Ran-GTP in the nucleus and Ran-GDP in the cytosol
options.C: Ran-GDP in the nucleus and Ran-GTP in the cytosol
options.D: SRP binding the NLS in the cytosol
options.E: An H⁺ gradient across the nuclear envelope

questions.explanation: Ran-GEF is bound to chromatin in the nucleus (makes Ran-GTP) and Ran-GAP is cytosolic (makes Ran-GDP); this gradient drives both import and export. A: Nucleoporins aren't ATP-driven pumps. C: Reversed: GEF is nuclear, GAP is cytosolic. D: SRP targets proteins to the ER; NLSs bind nuclear import receptors. E: An H⁺ gradient drives mitochondrial, not nuclear, import.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 18, 20–21

questions.stem: A drug collapses the H⁺ gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which step of protein import is directly blocked?

options.A: Signal-sequence translocation through TIM into the matrix

questions.explanation: Translocation of the signal sequence across the inner membrane into the matrix requires the electrochemical H⁺ gradient. B: Release of cytosolic hsp70 depends on ATP hydrolysis, not the H⁺ gradient. C: TOM recognition at the outer membrane comes first and doesn't need the gradient. D: Translation is unaffected. E: Glycosylation is an ER event.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 26–27

questions.stem: A soluble ER chaperone escapes to the Golgi. How is it returned to the ER?

options.A: Its KKXX signal binds COPI coats directly
options.B: The KDEL receptor packages it into COPII vesicles
options.C: The M6P receptor packages it into clathrin vesicles
options.D: The KDEL receptor packages it into COPI vesicles
options.E: Its NLS binds a nuclear import receptor

questions.explanation: Soluble ER residents carry a C-terminal KDEL; the KDEL receptor (high affinity in the Golgi, low in the ER) packages them into retrograde COPI vesicles. A: KKXX binding COPI directly is the route for ER membrane proteins. B: COPII carries cargo forward from ER to Golgi. C: M6P sorts lysosomal hydrolases. E: NLSs target the nucleus.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 51–52

questions.stem: A mutation blocks assembly of COPII coats. What is the most direct consequence?

options.A: Newly made secretory proteins accumulate in the ER
options.B: Escaped ER residents accumulate in the Golgi
options.C: Lysosomal hydrolases are secreted into the blood
options.D: Nuclear proteins remain in the cytosol
options.E: LDL stays bound at the cell surface

questions.explanation: Proteins leave the ER in COPII-coated vesicles, so blocking COPII traps cargo in the ER. B: That would follow a COPI/retrieval defect. C: That is I-cell disease (missing M6P tag). D: That is an NLS/import defect. E: That is a clathrin-coated pit defect.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 44, 50–51

questions.stem: A 1-year-old has coarse facies and skeletal abnormalities. Fibroblasts show large lysosomal inclusions, and plasma lysosomal enzyme activities are markedly elevated. Which feature of these enzymes is normally recognized for tagging?
questions.explanation: I-cell disease: GlcNAc phosphotransferase recognizes a signal patch on lysosomal hydrolases and starts M6P tagging; without it, hydrolases are secreted into the blood. A: KDEL retains soluble ER proteins. B: The N-terminal signal sends them into the ER but doesn't sort them to lysosomes. C: A C-terminal 3-amino-acid signal targets peroxisomes. D: Lysine-rich internal signals are NLSs.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 12, 57–59

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man eats home-canned vegetables and develops descending flaccid paralysis. The toxin cleaves proteins needed for vesicle fusion at the NMJ. Which protein family is targeted?
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNAREs, which catalyze vesicle fusion with the target membrane, so ACh isn't released. A: Clathrin coats endocytic and TGN vesicles. C: Targeting GTPases help guide vesicles but aren't the toxin target. D: COPII acts at the ER. E: Adaptins link clathrin to cargo receptors.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 47–48

questions.stem: A precursor protein moves from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix. Which transport mode is this, and what must the protein do?
questions.explanation: Transmembrane transport: translocators move proteins into a topologically distinct space (ER lumen, mitochondria), and the protein usually must unfold to snake through. A, D: Gated transport is nucleus–cytosol traffic through pores. B: Vesicular transport moves cargo between topologically equivalent compartments (e.g. ER → Golgi). E: Mitochondrial precursors are imported unfolded.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 6–8, 25

questions.stem: A protein's only sorting signal is an N-terminal sequence containing 5–10 hydrophobic amino acids. Where does it most likely end up?
questions.explanation: An N-terminal hydrophobic signal targets the protein to the ER via SRP; without further signals it passes to the Golgi and on to the cell surface by default. A: ER retention needs a C-terminal KDEL. B: Mitochondrial signals alternate positive and hydrophobic residues. C: Peroxisomal signals are C-terminal 3-amino-acid sequences. D: NLSs are internal clusters of positive residues.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 12, 33, 63
